source: Fleming (2001) Recombinant uncertainty in technological search, Management Science 47(1):117-132 (full text re-opened from the Berkeley Fung Institute copy)
finding: Gap 9 closed for this paper: the full text is freely available and the numbers used in our claims match it. More familiar components and more familiar combinations raise mean citations. Familiar components cut spread, then raise it again at the extreme.
numbers: n = 17,264 US patents granted May/June 1990; citations counted after July 1990. Component familiarity: +11.3% expected citations per SD, +147% from lowest to highest value (2.28). Combination familiarity: +10.3% per SD, +332% at max (11.25). Spread: component familiarity cuts variance 9.6% at the 60th percentile, effect turns positive at the 96th percentile (hypothesis 2 fails). Combination familiarity cuts variance 2.2% at the mean (0.28) and 64% at the max. Cumulative use of one combination: 37.9% of baseline citations at the max of 26.76; -5.6% per SD. Mean citation count 3.80.
quote: cannot definitively separate learning and familiarity, technological exhaustion, and life-cycle effects
limits: One cohort of two months. Random half splits kept the signs but not always the significance. Subclass pairs are a proxy for components. Citation community differences across fields.
agent_relevance: The numbers behind O7 reuse rules are now checked against the primary text. The cohort is old and narrow, so use the direction, not the sizes.

source: Fleming (2001), what the paper says about its own mean result for new combinations
finding: The 'lower mean for novel pairs' claim is carried by the familiarity coefficients, not by a separate test of new pairs against old. Familiarity helps the mean; a negative effect of novelty is the mirror reading of that.
numbers: Combination familiarity coefficient on the mean is positive and highly significant (see d01). Hypothesis 2 on component-level spread is not supported by the author's own text. Hypothesis 5 (exhaustion) is supported by a negative cumulative-use coefficient.
limits: The author warns the models cannot split exhaustion from life-cycle decline; exhaustion is therefore not shown as causal.
agent_relevance: Treat 'novel pairs cost mean usefulness' as an inference from familiarity gains. Test it directly in any agent experiment.

source: Uzzi, Mukherjee, Stringer, Jones (2013) Atypical combinations and scientific impact, Science 342:468 (published text re-opened)
finding: Gap 9 team-share discrepancy settled. The printed Figure 3 caption gives 36.2%, 39.9%, 49.7% (solo, two authors, three or more). The earlier 36.1% and 39.8% in evidence a08 were transcription slips.
numbers: Tail novelty (10th-percentile z below 0) in 36.2%, 39.9%, 49.7% of solo, dual, 3+ author papers. The text states teams are 37.7% more likely than solo to insert novel combinations (the ratio of the rounded shares gives 37.3%, so the paper uses unrounded values). Hit rate per 100: 9.11 for conventional core + novel tail. 17.9 million papers. Robustness (time periods, fig S4; definition of hit, fig S5; each of 243 fields, fig S6 and table S2) is stated in the main text; the supplement itself was not opened.
limits: Supplement figures not opened. Association only.
agent_relevance: Use 36.2/39.9/49.7 in all notes. The finding that mixes a conventional core with a small novel tail stands.

source: Foster, Rzhetsky, Evans (2015) Tradition and innovation in scientists' research strategies, American Sociological Review (manuscript text re-opened)
finding: Gap 9 closed for this paper. Scientists mostly repeat. Rarer moves earn more citations on average and have higher spread, but the paper can only bound the failure rate, since it sees only projects that were published.
numbers: Repeat statements 85.8% versus new or jump 14.2%. New bridges and new consolidations 12.4% versus jumps 1.8%. A strategy an order of magnitude less probable (0.5 vs 0.05) gets 2.26 more citations on average. Surprisal explains 29.2% of the variation in mean citations and 28.6% of the variation in the standard deviation of citations.
limits: Failed projects are not observed. The risk bound assumes scientists maximise citations. Biomedical chemistry (MEDLINE) data.
agent_relevance: Supports a small far-move share as the observed human norm (about 14%) and the 'higher mean AND higher spread' form of Fleming for papers. It does not give an optimum for an agent.

source: Verhoeven, Bakker, Veugelers (2016) Measuring technological novelty with patent-based indicators, Research Policy 45:707 (regression tables 10-11 re-read)
finding: Gap 10 mostly closed. This is a direct same-model replication of Fleming (generalized negative binomial models of mean and dispersion) on a different source: PATSTAT worldwide patent families to 2003. With controls, new recombination lowers the mean and raises spread, as Fleming said. Evidence b19 wrongly said the mean was not tested.
numbers: Mean / dispersion coefficients: new recombination NR -0.0957 / +0.0942 (about -9.1% citations); new technological origins NTO -0.127 / +0.0419 (about -11.9%); new scientific origins NSO +0.0469 / not significant (about +4.8%). NR+NTO+NSO together: +0.0463 / +0.0909 (the only combination with a higher mean). NR and NSO: -0.0988 mean. N = 2,340,607 (model 1) and 3,604,932 (models 2-4). 7-year citation window. Pseudo R-squared about 0.042-0.043.
limits: Patent families, not single national patents. Citation counts as impact. Controls (family size, filings, 35 technology fields) matter, see d06.
agent_relevance: Patent-side evidence now supports both halves of Fleming: lower mean for new pairs (after controls) and higher spread. Plan the agent policy around a wider spread, with a known mean cost.

source: Verhoeven et al. (2016), raw forward-citation means (Table 10)
finding: Without controls the sign flips. Novel patent families get MORE citations on average than non-novel ones, and the most novel (all three flags) have the highest spread. So the mean penalty only shows after holding family size and field fixed.
numbers: Mean (SD) forward citations, scoring 0 vs 1: any novelty 6.03 (9.83) vs 6.62 (11.02); NR 6.60 vs 6.66; NSO 6.11 vs 10.74 (SD 9.93 vs 18.99); all three 6.17 (10.09) vs 12.96 (21.72, N = 12,471). Difference of means significant at p < 0.001. About 25% of families score on at least one flag; under 1% on all three.
limits: Descriptive. Novel families are also larger families, which inflates raw counts.
agent_relevance: A raw comparison of blended versus plain outputs can show a gain from novelty that vanishes once cost and length are controlled. Control for output length and tokens.

source: Wu, Wang, Evans (2019) Large teams develop and small teams disrupt science and technology, Nature (manuscript text re-opened)
finding: Gap 8 (human side). Bigger teams produce more hits but less disruption. Solo authors are as likely as five-person teams to produce a top-5% cited paper, yet 72% more likely to produce a top-5% disruptive one. Singh-Fleming's 'cut the poor tail, lift the good tail' is about citations, not disruption, and does not extend to disruption.
numbers: More than 50 million papers, patents and software products, 1954-2014 (43 million Web of Science articles, 615 million citations). Ten-person teams 50% more likely to score a hit (top 5% citations). Disruption falls with each added member. Fusing surprising journal combinations saturates at 8 to 10 members and then reverses, dropping below solo and small teams.
limits: Part of the gap is topic and resources. An author fixed-effects check is reported. Teams here are co-authors, not independent searchers.
agent_relevance: Do not assume more agents always give more novel results. A fixed small number of independent searches, then a merge, matches the saturation at 8 to 10.

source: Singh and Fleming (2010) Lone inventors as sources of breakthroughs: myth or reality? Management Science 56(1):41-56 (abstract only; full text not reachable)
finding: Gap 8 stays open. Full text was not obtained: INFORMS returned HTTP 403, and the HAL record that a search tool linked turned out to be a different paper (tennis rackets). The abstract-level claims are: over half a million patents, lone inventors are less likely to produce breakthroughs and more likely to produce very poor outcomes, shown with quantile regressions; the team effect is partly mediated by diversity of team members' technical experience and size of their external networks; experience diversity mainly cuts the poor tail.
numbers: Abstract-level only: more than 500,000 patented inventions. No coefficients obtained.
limits: Not opened. Do not quote numbers from it.

source: Jiang et al. (2025) Artificial Hivemind: the open-ended homogeneity of language models, NeurIPS Datasets and Benchmarks (arXiv 2510.22954)
finding: Gap 8 and gap 7 (LLM side). Many independent samples, even from different model families, land on nearly the same ideas. Several agents drawn from similar models are not independent searchers.
numbers: 26K open-ended prompts, 70+ models (25 shown). One model at top-p 0.9, temperature 1.0: in 79% of cases the average pairwise embedding similarity of its answers exceeds 0.8. With min-p decoding at temperature 2.0: 81% of pairs still above 0.7, 61.2% above 0.8. Between different models the average pairwise similarity is 71% to 82% (DeepSeek-V3 and qwen-max 0.82; DeepSeek-V3 and gpt-4o 0.81). 25 models x 50 responses to 'write a metaphor about time' form two clusters.
limits: Embedding similarity of text (text-embedding-3-small), not an outcome check. Open-ended prompts, not search problems.
agent_relevance: Spread across agents must come from different inputs (different part sets, different source domains), not from re-running one prompt on several models.

source: Bao, Wu, Liu, Li, Cao, Evans (2026) Contemporary AI lacks the imagination to diverge or negate in science (arXiv 2606.08251), stylised simulation
finding: A simulation (not data) of studies that all use an error-correlated AI instrument: the uncorrelated part of error shrinks with more AI throughput, but the shared bias never averages out, so total error can rise.
numbers: In the stylised model, the net-knowledge measure is 0.47 with null suppression on versus 0.76 with it off. The averageable-variance band narrows and the shared part widens as AI share rises.
limits: Author-built model with chosen parameters. Not a test of recombination.
agent_relevance: Supports gap 8 from the theory side: voting over agents with shared errors reduces noise only in the part that is not shared.

source: Hope, Chan, Kittur, Shahaf (2017) Accelerating innovation through analogy mining, KDD (arXiv 1706.05585)
finding: Gaps 1, 4, 5. Inspirations that are near in purpose and far in mechanism, spread out with a max-min rule, gave a higher rate of good ideas than surface-similar inspirations or random ones. Surface-near retrieval was no better than random.
numbers: 38 Mechanical Turk workers, 12 seed products, 749 ideas, 5 graduate-student judges (Fleiss kappa 0.51). Shared-seed slice (9 seeds), good-idea share, at least 2 of 5 judges: analogy condition 46% (N=105) vs random 37% (49) vs TF-IDF surface 30% (54), p<.01. Majority vote (3 of 5): 38% vs 22% vs 21%. Model estimate of P(good), k=2: 0.71 [0.48, 0.87] vs TF-IDF 0.28 vs random 0.27; k=3: 0.56 vs 0.16 vs 0.14. Each person saw 12 inspirations after one minute of unaided ideation.
limits: Humans, not LLMs. Wide intervals, small sample. The authors state results could land between the arms with more data.
agent_relevance: Direct template for O7: choose parts near on the goal, far on the mechanism, and diversify. Measure usefulness by a judge panel or a check, not by distance alone.

source: Hu et al. (2024) Nova: an iterative planning and search approach to enhance novelty and diversity of LLM-generated ideas (arXiv 2410.14255)
finding: Gap 2 (LLM). Novelty gains from repeated retrieve-and-revise rounds come early and stop after three. Without planned retrieval the count of unique novel ideas does not grow between rounds 2 and 3.
numbers: 3 rounds, 15 seed ideas, 3x more seeds each round, 405 seeds clustered to 100 final ideas per paper, 170 seed papers. Unique novel ideas 3.4 times higher than without the framework. Ablation (K = 5 retrieved papers): no planning 42.4 then 44.1 unique novel ideas at steps 2 and 3; no planning and no retrieval 25.3, 30.6, 31.35 at steps 1-3. 619 ideas scored 4 and 2,521 scored 5 on a Swiss tournament; human panel of 10 experts gave Nova 37.5% of the top four places. Authors say there was no continued increment after 3 rounds.
limits: Novelty is judged by an LLM and an embedding threshold (0.3 for novelty, 0.8 for duplicates), not by an outcome check. Equal output count (100 ideas per method), not equal compute. Each round adds new outside knowledge, not only refinement.
agent_relevance: Cap refinement at about 2 to 3 rounds and add new input each round; a round that adds no new input stalls.

source: Chen, Zhang, Li et al. (2025) Structuring scientific innovation: modeling and discovering impactful knowledge combinations (arXiv 2503.18865)
finding: Gaps 1 and 5. A search over problem-method pairs that mostly picks the best-scoring move but, with a small probability, accepts a random one found more high-disruption pairs than pure greedy search and than prompting three frontier LLMs.
numbers: Hit rate (disruption index above 0.5), DBLP / PubMed / PatSnap: GPT-4o 16.4 / 18.2 / 14.9; Claude 3.5 15.7 / 17.1 / 14.3; Claude 3.7 17.2 / 19.0 / 15.6; standard greedy 19.3 / 21.5 / 18.2; greedy + probabilistic perturbation 26.3 / 28.1 / 24.6 (about 7 points over greedy). Data: 14,533 AI papers 2011-2021; 96,612 depression papers 2015-2025; 6,677 medical-robotics patents 2020-2025.
limits: The perturbation probability is not stated in the text read. The optimised index comes from the authors' own predictor, and the text does not make clear whether the hit rate is scored on true disruption. Compute is not matched across arms. Single group.
agent_relevance: Supports a small random-move share inside an otherwise greedy search; gives no number for the share. Needs an outcome check on the final choice.

source: Mizrahi, Shani, Stanovsky, Jurafsky, Shahaf (2025) Cooking up creativity (arXiv 2504.20643): budget check on the baseline
finding: Gap 1 stays open. The strongest explicit-recombination study compares its top 5 out of a very large pool with 5 recipes from one prompted session. No best-of-N arm at equal tokens exists.
numbers: Up to 5,600 blended trees per dish pair (5.5 million in all); top 5 per pair kept. Baseline GPT-4o: 104 and 114 prompt variants tried, the best prompt chosen by two chefs, temperature 1, one chat session. One pipeline step cost about $42. Results: tree edit distance 132.14 vs 89.35 (Exp 1) and 140.25 vs 129.55 (Exp 2) in favour of the pipeline; self-BLEU-2 0.423 vs 0.726 (Exp 1), 0.778 vs 0.902 (Exp 2). 48 Prolific raters, 5 per recipe, Krippendorff alpha 0.201 and 0.209.
limits: Selection from 5,600 vs 5 is a huge unequal draw. Rater agreement is low. Domain is recipes with no verified outcome.
agent_relevance: Do not cite this as proof that recombination beats sampling. Run best-of-N with the same tokens and a verified outcome.

source: Liu, Dubova, Conklin, Harada, Griffiths (2026) Assessing the effect of cross-domain mapping on creativity in humans and LLMs (arXiv 2603.19087): distance threshold and open-weight models
finding: Gap 6 partly answered. For LLMs as a group the supplied far source first hurt originality against a plain user-need prompt; the gap closed and stopped being significant after the nearest 20% of pairs were dropped. For the two best models a gain appears only at the far end. One task only.
numbers: Seven LLMs (o3, Claude-Sonnet-4, gpt-4o, gemini-2.5-pro, deepseek-v3, Llama-3.3-70b, Qwen2.5-72B). o3 and Claude-Sonnet-4: all pairs effect 0.02 (p=.64); most distant 50%: 0.12 (p=.029); most distant 10%: 0.24 (p=.024). Llama-3.3-70b did not reliably beat humans on originality. The three open-weight models were not analysed alone for the threshold.
limits: One task (product ideation from an object plus a source domain), originality ratings, human raters. No per-open-weight threshold.
agent_relevance: A far-source step is worth its tokens only when the pair is distant enough; otherwise a plain prompt matches or beats it. Use a distance gate.

source: Kombine benchmark (arXiv 2509.21043): does embedding distance predict quality?
finding: Gap 4. At the model level, embedding-distance originality of far associations predicts other facets, including how often a model finds a valid blend.
numbers: 35 LLMs. Association originality correlates with analogy originality r=0.73 (p<1e-4), analogy surprise 0.63, blend originality 0.42, blend surprise 0.50, valid blends 0.48 (p=3e-3). Mean cross-task correlation 0.47. Paper states the pattern holds across embedding model choices (appendix not opened). Valid generic space found 43.4% of the time; given one, coherent blend 97.1%.
limits: Model-level correlations with 35 points, not item-level prediction of usefulness. Constructed items.
agent_relevance: Embedding distance is a usable ranking signal across models but is not shown to predict item usefulness; pair it with a validity check.

source: Chen, Zhao, Cohan (2026) Measuring the gap between human and LLM research ideas (arXiv 2607.01233)
finding: Gaps 3 and 5. LLM research ideas lean heavily on recombination framing already. Turning on thinking mode makes it worse.
numbers: 11,683 matched papers (5,994 ML, 5,689 Nature Communications). Bridge or fragmentation opportunities: 12.1% of human ideas vs 47.1% to 64.2% across nine LLMs. Explicit synthesis or unification as the main method: 5.1% human vs 22.5% to 38.7%. Qwen3-8B with thinking: bridge 49.7% to 71.1%, synthesis 38.7% to 52.2%, opportunity entropy 0.658 to 0.481, distance from human distribution (TVD) 0.382 to 0.590. DeepSeek-V4-Flash: bridge 52.2% to 59.1%, synthesis 22.5% to 30.7%.
limits: Label taxonomy applied by LLM annotation. Prompts give a small set of prior papers. No outcome check.
agent_relevance: A blend step adds to a habit the model already has. Budget the blend step and keep a non-blend branch (new problem framing).

source: ReMIND (Sato, 2026, arXiv 2601.07121): wake, dream, judge, rewake
finding: Gaps 2 and 3, weak. High-temperature exploration moves outputs away from the low-temperature baseline, but temperature does not control how far. A judge acts mostly as a novelty filter, and gains come in two separable steps, exploration and then consolidation.
numbers: Dream temperatures 1, 3, 10. Wake-wake similarity near 1.0; wake-dream similarity spread widely in all four model sets. Judge consistency scores skewed to the maximum of 5; pass rates under 50% in some sets because rewake was skipped when no novel idea was found.
limits: Novelty scores come from other LLMs, no outcome check, small tasks. Cited for design only.
agent_relevance: Keeps the sample-wide, then-consolidate order. Not evidence on rounds.

source: Katila and Ahuja (2002) Something old, something new, Academy of Management Journal 45(6) (record only)
finding: Gap 10 stays open for this paper. Semantic Scholar lists it (about 3,500 citations) with no open PDF. Only the metadata was seen. Fleming-Sorenson 2001 and Kaplan-Vakili 2015 are in the same state.
numbers: Metadata only: 2002 publication, citation count about 3,507 in the main record.
limits: Not read. Do not use any finding from it.
agent_relevance: Leave K25 and the Katila-Ahuja line marked unread.
